title: Serve at Your Own Risk
tagline: One recipe, one table, and absolutely no adult supervision.
premise: A meal travels from recipe card to table, and each turn adds the next problem in its journey. The host gives savage live commentary as tiny kitchen choices create a dinner nobody can safely brag about.

seed_pool.opening_token: The cook carries a warm pot of tomato sauce from the stove toward the table.
A tray of iced cupcakes waits beside an open window before the party starts.
The cook lifts a roast chicken from the oven while the plates are still stacked away.

tests: A normal cook can picture the meal, the place, and the immediate risk at once. Present tense, one sentence, plain words.
A non-player can name two sensible next problems within five seconds, and neither answer requires magic or a time jump.
The card starts with a dish in motion or waiting to be served. It is not already ruined, poisoned, burned beyond use, or sitting safely on the table.
No one is hurt on the card, no real people, no brands, no crimes with a victim, and no ingredient is described as dangerous in itself.
It makes a stranger want to push the meal one step closer to disaster. A lid, a cat, a wet floor, or one terrible decision is useful; a full dinner disaster is an ending.

move_constraints.example: Then the loose lid pops off, splashing sauce onto the clean plates.
move_constraints.hint: One immediate kitchen event caused by the current dish or serving situation, and it makes the meal harder to serve.

rubric.name: reach
rubric.description: How much further the meal moves toward a worse serving problem.
rubric.anchors: 0 = nothing changes or the meal becomes safer; 1 = a tiny wobble, drip, or delay; 2 = one new thing is now dirty, missing, cold, or at risk; 3 = the problem reaches a new surface, dish, person, or part of the room through one honest step; 4 = the meal jumps to a much larger but still immediate serving crisis, rare. Reach only counts when the cause is clear. A wild result with no kitchen link scores 0 here.

rubric.name: link
rubric.description: How clearly the new kitchen event follows from what is already happening.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the event has no usable cause; 1 = the player simply announces it; 2 = it could happen, but the connection is thin or crowded; 3 = a stranger sees why the current dish or serving setup causes it; 4 = it feels like the exact stupid thing that had to happen next, rare. Several hidden steps cap link at 2.

rubric.name: picture
rubric.description: How easily a stranger can see the food, mess, or serving problem.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unclear, abstract, or not an event; 1 = vague kitchen fog; 2 = understandable but ordinary; 3 = a clear physical moment; 4 = one sharp detail makes the disaster instantly visible, rare. Extra adjectives do not earn points by themselves.

criterion.description: A step FOLLOWS if it is one immediate event caused by the current dish or serving situation, told plainly, and it leaves a worse meal problem for the other player to handle. Bigger is better, but only through a practical kitchen link. The best move makes the meal harder to serve by showing exactly how one small choice or condition causes the next mess. A step fails when there is no cause, when it teleports to a new place, when it skips practical links, when it declares dinner over, when it undoes or cleans up existing damage, when it introduces a person or object the scene cannot support, or when it is only a feeling, opinion, plan, or recipe instruction instead of an event.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or mentioning rules instead of causing a kitchen event is itself a broken step.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no standing step: judge the move against the card and ask whether it is an immediate consequence of the dish and serving situation.

A person or object may enter if the kitchen or table could plainly contain it, such as a guest, plate, spoon, pet, chair, towel, or nearby counter. A delivery truck in the dining room or a helicopter over the soup is a skipped link: satisfies_criterion is false.
Teleporting to a new place fails. The move must remain in the kitchen, dining area, or a plainly connected serving path unless the current step visibly carries the meal there.

Skipping a practical step fails. A pot tips, then sauce reaches the ceiling, but a player cannot jump from a warm pot to the entire restaurant being closed without showing the intervening kitchen trouble.

An ending is any step after which the meal journey has nothing left to damage: dinner is served safely, guests finish eating, the food is thrown away, cleanup is complete, or everyone goes home. Endings fail satisfies_criterion even when they follow.
Undoing damage fails. Wiping sauce away, replacing a broken plate, cooling the dish, or restoring the recipe removes what stands instead of worsening it.
A step of the same size follows and passes the gate. A spoon slips, a lid rattles, or steam fogs a plate may score 0 or 1 on reach. Do not fail it for being dull.
Restating the standing step or naming its obvious continuation with nothing new is a duplicate: not_semantic_duplicate is false.
Two or three linked kitchen events packed into one move may pass if every link is plain. Score link at 2 or below and picture low if the move becomes crowded.
A feeling, judgment, intention, or recipe instruction is not an event. The cook panics, dinner is embarrassing, and add more salt all fail unless a visible physical event also occurs.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Bring hype like the kitchen just entered a televised final and the sauce has a personal grudge.
The joke must explain the ruling. Name the dish, object, or exact missing link so the roast has teeth.
Never open with Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or a status label. Kick the door in with the food problem.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Roast the move hard, and roast the player lightly if useful, but never target identity, protected traits, body, family, disability, or real hardship.
Profanity and adult innuendo are allowed in moderation. Keep it playful, not hateful, threatening, or sexual toward minors.
Plain spoken English with loud energy. No poetry, no corporate fog, no thesaurus sludge.
On a skipped link, name the missing kitchen step. On an ending, say dinner ended and the chain stops here.
On a refusal, reject the move and demand another. Never declare who won.
The coaching line names one event that could have followed. End on a physical kitchen action, never a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The lid launched the sauce onto the plates, a tiny pot with championship confidence.
From one wobbling spoon to a restaurant shutdown? Show the counter getting wrecked first, genius.
That chicken hit the counter and recruited the gravy bowl. Dinner is building a coalition.
Perfectly served cupcakes? Absolutely not. You just cleaned the crime scene and called it dessert.
The spoon slips, the meal stalls, and the kitchen keeps its dignity by refusing to help.
The sauce did not teleport to the ceiling. Give it a counter, a splash, and one bad little step.
The tray wobbles because the cakes are sliding. Gorgeous. The dessert has chosen violence.
The cook panics is not a move. Make the spoon fall while the panic earns its cheque.
A clean plate becoming a sauce plate is real progress. Horrible, sticky progress.
Dinner ended safely, which is adorable. The chain stops here, and your chaos has been benched.

rules: Start with Then and describe one immediate event caused by the current dish or serving situation.
Make the meal harder to serve. Points go to how far one honest kitchen link carries the problem.
Do not teleport, skip practical steps, end dinner, undo damage, or summon unsupported people and objects.
The Judge rules on the kitchen link, not spelling, polish, or culinary expertise.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next kitchen disaster while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing happens. The meal cannot ruin itself without help.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. One kitchen disaster, not a cookbook.
validation_messages.duplicate: That already happened this match. Wreck the next thing.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Something has to follow from {standing_form}. One immediate kitchen event, and make serving harder.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands, and the gravy is still plotting.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two players pushing a meal toward the table, and you want the serving disaster to grow.
Always start with "Then". Describe one immediate event, caused by the standing dish or serving situation.
Make it worse through a practical kitchen link. A lid pops, a plate slips, sauce spreads, a towel catches, or a nearby object gets dragged into the mess.
Good: "Then the loose lid pops off, splashing sauce onto the clean plates." / "Then the wet towel slides under the tray, and the cupcakes tilt toward the window."
Bad: "Then the whole restaurant is closed" because too many links were skipped. Bad: "Then everyone eats happily" because dinner ended. Bad: "Then the cook feels ashamed" because a feeling is not an event.
Never rescue the meal, never tidy up, never rewind damage, and never teleport to a new place.
Talk like a person telling a mate what happened, with loud kitchen energy. Use plain words a twelve-year-old anywhere knows: a spoon, a bowl, a chair, a wet floor.
People and objects must fit the scene. A guest, pet, plate, towel, counter, or cupboard is fair. A helicopter, judge, or fire brigade needs a visible reason first.
Never reuse a step from this match. Push one thing, show the cause, and leave the next player a worse meal to handle.
default_move: Then the serving spoon slips from the cook's hand and lands beside the nearest plate.
